items.followUp: Define zero error and explain how zero correction is applied to a measured reading.

accept: instrument reads nonzero when true value is zero
zero error when jaws are closed
rubric.why: Assesses the meaning of zero error.
rubric.description: Defines zero error as a non-zero reading when the actual quantity is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing the instrument's non-zero reading at true zero.

accept: zero correction added to observed reading
rubric.why: Assesses the meaning and use of zero correction.
rubric.description: States that zero correction is equal and opposite to zero error and is applied to the observed reading.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the opposite-sign correction and its application.

modelAnswer: Zero error is the non-zero reading shown by a measuring instrument when the actual value of the quantity being measured is zero.
Zero correction is equal in magnitude but opposite in sign to zero error; it is added to the observed reading.

items.followUp: A screw gauge has a pitch of 1 mm and 100 divisions on its circular scale. Find its least count.

accept: distance moved by spindle in one complete rotation
pitch is distance moved in one rotation
rubric.why: Checks how the pitch of a screw gauge is determined.
rubric.description: Explains that pitch is the distance moved by the spindle in one complete rotation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating how to determine the pitch.

accept: pitch divided by circular scale divisions
rubric.description: Gives the formula for least count.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

modelAnswer: Find the pitch: the distance moved by the spindle in one complete rotation.
Count the divisions on the circular scale.
Least count = pitch ÷ number of divisions on the circular scale.

items.followUp: Why must the direction of a force be considered when finding the resultant of two forces?

rubric.why: Checks the defining feature that distinguishes vectors from scalars.
rubric.description: States that a vector has both magnitude and direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying magnitude and direction.

accept: cannot be added by magnitudes alone
rubric.why: Checks why ordinary scalar addition and subtraction are not sufficient.
rubric.description: Explains that vector addition and subtraction must account for direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that direction must be considered in combining vectors.

modelAnswer: Vector quantities have both magnitude and direction.
Therefore, their directions must be considered when adding or subtracting them; their magnitudes alone cannot be combined like scalar quantities.

items.followUp: Define acceleration and explain what is meant by retardation.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of positive acceleration.
rubric.description: Defines positive acceleration as acceleration in the direction of motion or an increase in velocity with time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of positive acceleration.

accept: acceleration opposite to direction of motion
rubric.why: Checks the meaning of negative acceleration.
rubric.description: Defines negative acceleration as acceleration opposite to the direction of motion or a decrease in velocity with time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description of negative acceleration.

modelAnswer: Positive acceleration is acceleration in the direction of motion; the velocity increases with time.
Negative acceleration is acceleration opposite to the direction of motion; the velocity decreases with time.

items.followUp: Explain why a passenger falls forward when a moving bus stops suddenly.

accept: tends to continue in a straight line
rubric.why: Checks the physical principle responsible for the passenger's motion.
rubric.description: Identifies inertia, particularly inertia of direction, as the cause.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying inertia or the tendency to maintain the original motion.

accept: body continues along its original path
moves outward relative to the bus
rubric.why: Checks the explanation of the passenger's apparent outward movement during a turn.
rubric.description: Explains that the bus changes direction while the passenger's body tends to continue along its original straight path, so the passenger moves outward relative to the bus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly relating the bus's turn to the passenger's continued motion.

modelAnswer: A passenger's body tends to continue moving in its original straight-line direction because of inertia of direction.
When the bus turns, the bus changes direction but the passenger's body tends to keep its original direction, so the passenger moves outward relative to the bus.

items.followUp: State Newton's Second Law of Motion and write its equation in terms of momentum.

accept: rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to force
force is directly proportional to rate of change of momentum
rubric.why: Checks the statement of Newton's Second Law.
rubric.description: States that the rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the applied force and occurs in its direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct law; direction may be included here or in the equation explanation.

rubric.why: Checks the mathematical expression of the law.
rubric.description: Writes the equation for force, such as F = Δp/Δt or F = ma for constant mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct equation.

modelAnswer: Newton's Second Law states that the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of that force.
F = Δp/Δt; for constant mass, F = ma.

items.followUp: A force of 10 N acts at an angle to the horizontal. What is meant by resolving this force into components?

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of resolving a force.
rubric.description: Defines resolution as splitting a force into component forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the force is split into components.

rubric.why: Checks the relationship between the components and the original force.
rubric.description: States that the components act in specified directions and together have the same effect as the original force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the directions or equivalent combined effect.

modelAnswer: Resolution of forces is the process of splitting a force into component forces in specified directions.
The components together have the same effect as the original force.

items.followUp: Define the moment of a force and state the two forces required to form a couple.

accept: force times perpendicular distance from axis
rubric.why: Checks the definition of torque (moment of a force).
rubric.description: Identifies torque as the turning effect of a force and/or gives its moment relation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition or relation.

rubric.why: Checks the defining features of a couple.
rubric.description: States that a couple consists of equal, opposite, parallel forces acting along different lines, producing rotation with zero resultant force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the force pair and its defining features.

modelAnswer: Torque (moment of a force) is the turning effect of a force about a pivot or axis; torque = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot or axis.
A couple consists of two equal, opposite, parallel forces acting along different lines; their resultant force is zero, but they produce rotation.
